chunks: "Source termination matches the driver to the line, so the driver's output impedance plus any series resistor equals Z 0 .
The wave goes out at half amplitude, the receiver end is high impedance so it doubles, and any reflection that comes back is absorbed at the source.
Sink termination matches the receiver: a resistor equal to Z 0 at the end of the line absorbs the wave as soon as it arrives, so nothing reflects at all.
The trade-offs: source termination is cheap and burns no DC power, but the signal only reaches full amplitude after a round trip, so it is for one receiver at the end.
Sink termination gives a clean, fast wave to every receiver along the way, tolerates a driver with the wrong impedance, but costs DC power and drives a reduced swing.
Sink termination also works as a bus: put it at the end of the line. Doing both is double termination, which is the RF standard: source and load both 50 ohms.
Any residual error at one end is absorbed by the other, so it's very forgiving, but the amplitude is only half of the source voltage.
That's fine for low-swing differential links and memory with on-die termination, but not for full-swing 3. 3 volts CMOS, which would only see 1. 65 volts.
For bidirectional buses like DDR every chip acts as both source and sink, so you use termination at the receiving end each time, which is exactly what on-die termination does."
